handsOnLab.brief: You will inventory a real Windows machine's running processes with PowerShell, classify each binary as known-good or unknown using signature and publisher data, and write the minute-by-minute decision trace showing which NIST-model gate would fire against a simulated attack chain. This turns the architecture from a diagram into an operator artifact.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Every binary in the CSV has a classification; every attack step in trace.md names a specific gate and verdict; no blanket path exceptions remain in policy-decisions.md.
handsOnLab.deliverable: A folder containing process-inventory.csv, policy-decisions.md, and trace.md — your machine's allowlist baseline plus the attack trace.
steps: On a Windows test machine, open PowerShell as Administrator and run Get-Process | Select-Object Name, Path | Sort-Object Name | Format-Table -AutoSize to list running processes.
For each unique executable path, run Get-AuthenticodeSignature <path> and record the SignerCertificate subject (publisher) and Status (Valid/NotSigned).
Export the inventory to CSV: build a small loop writing Name, Path, Publisher, SignatureStatus to process-inventory.csv.
Classify each row: KNOWN-GOOD (valid signature from a recognized publisher AND business-needed), REVIEW (valid signature but unknown publisher or unneeded), UNKNOWN (unsigned or hash-only).
Write policy-decisions.md: for each REVIEW/UNKNOWN binary, write the allow or deny decision with a one-line justification, as if you were the Policy Engine.

Draft the attack trace: on paper or in trace.md, write the 9:02 AM macro attack from the notes against YOUR inventory — name which of your actual running apps would be the initial vector and which gate fires at each step.
Identify your three riskiest REVIEW items and write the ringfence rule each would need (e.g., 'deny child process creation for <app>').
Write the offline-posture decision: if the agent cannot reach the policy server, do new executions fail closed or open on your design? Justify in two sentences.
Review policy-decisions.md and flag any rule shaped like 'allow everything in <folder>' — rewrite it as a scoped rule.
Read the finished trace.md end to end and confirm every attack step meets a named gate with a verdict.
handsOnLab.title: Build the deny-by-default decision trace

choices: On the protected machine the attack dies at the first gate it meets — ringfence blocks the macro's child-process spawn or allowlisting blocks the unknown binary before it runs, Detect alerts at the attempt stage, and network/storage gates contain lateral movement and exfiltration; on the default-allow machine nothing evaluates the payload until a signature fires after encryption has started.
Both machines behave the same until the antivirus signature updates, since allowlisting is just another signature list.
The protected machine encrypts faster because the agent consumes CPU; the default-allow machine is safer due to lower overhead.
The protected machine requires the user to approve each block in real time, so the outcome depends on the user clicking correctly.
mockTask.explain: This is the minute-by-minute trace from the notes: default-deny fails closed at the attempt stage with no threat intel required, while default-allow needs to recognize the threat — which happens after damage. Mention the five gates and the Detect alert to show operator depth.
mockTask.q: Panel question: 'Ransomware hits one of our endpoints at 9 AM. Walk me through what happens on a ThreatLocker-protected machine versus a traditional default-allow machine.'

notes.body: Zero trust is a set of design principles, not a product SKU. The core idea is simple and brutal: no user, device, application, or network segment is trusted by default — every access request is authenticated, authorized, and continuously re-evaluated. Location used to be trust. In the old castle-and-moat model, anything inside the corporate network was treated as friendly and anything outside as hostile. That model died the moment laptops left the building, VPNs became the front door, and attackers learned that phishing one employee puts them inside the moat. Zero trust moves the trust decision from 'where are you?' to 'who are you, what is the health of your device, and is this specific request legitimate right now?' NIST SP 800-207, the canonical reference, frames zero trust around a simple rule: all communication is secured regardless of network location, access is granted per session, and access decisions are driven by dynamic policy that considers client identity, the requesting asset's posture, and behavioral attributes. Notice what is missing from that list: 'because the request came from the office LAN.' There are three ideas people constantly confuse with zero trust, so let us separate them. First, zero trust is not 'no trust at all' — it is trust that is explicitly granted, narrowly scoped, and constantly re-verified. You still trust your identity provider, your policy engine, and your device health signals; you just stop trusting the network cable. Second, zero trust is not a firewall upgrade. A firewall is one enforcement point; zero trust is the architecture that coordinates all of them. Third, zero trust is not achieved by buying a platform — it is achieved by changing defaults: default-deny instead of default-allow, per-session authorization instead of login-once, and continuous diagnostics instead of annual audits. On the endpoint, the single most consequential default you can change is which applications are allowed to run. A default-allow endpoint runs whatever arrives; a default-deny endpoint runs only what policy explicitly permits. Everything ThreatLocker's allowlisting module does — and everything you will operate in this course — is zero trust applied to the question 'may this code execute on this machine?' Common operator gotcha: do not pitch zero trust to leadership or to an interview panel as a product. The panel on October 13 will respect you far more for saying 'zero trust is the discipline of removing implicit trust and enforcing per-session, policy-driven decisions, and here is how we applied it to application execution' than for naming vendors.
notes.title: What 'zero trust' actually means

notes.body: NIST SP 800-207 gives zero trust a logical anatomy with three named components, and you should be able to draw them from memory. The Policy Engine (PE) is the brain: it makes the ultimate decision to grant, deny, or revoke access to a resource, using enterprise policy plus inputs like identity, device posture, and threat intelligence. The Policy Administrator (PA) is the muscle that carries out the decision: it establishes and tears down the communication path between the subject and the resource, for example by generating session credentials or configuring the enforcement point. The Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) is the gate: it sits in the data path, enables or terminates connections, and enforces the PE's decision. The PE and PA together form the control plane; the PEP and the resource sit in the data plane. A trust algorithm inside the PE weighs the inputs — identity assurance level, device compliance state, behavioral anomalies — and produces the decision. Worked example, mapped to an endpoint: an accountant double-clicks invoicing-app.exe. The endpoint agent acting as PEP intercepts the execution request instead of letting it run. It asks the control plane: the PE evaluates policy ('is invoicing-app.exe on the allowlist for the accounting group? is the device compliant? is the file hash unchanged?') and the PA instructs the PEP to allow or block the launch. If allowed, the PEP permits that specific execution; it does not hand the app a permanent hall pass. That is the per-session idea applied to process execution. Now map the failure modes, because operators live in failure modes. If the PEP is bypassed — the app launches without consulting policy — the whole model collapses regardless of how good the PE is. If the PE's inputs are stale — device posture from last week — decisions are made on lies. If the PA cannot reach the PEP — the agent is offline — you need a defined offline posture: fail closed (block new executions) or fail open, and you must choose deliberately, document it, and be able to defend the choice. Common gotcha: people draw the PE, PA, and PEP as three boxes and stop. The interview-grade understanding is the data flow between them and what happens when each link breaks. Practice explaining it in sixty seconds: subject requests, PEP intercepts, PE decides with the trust algorithm, PA enforces, PEP gates. Then add: 'and on the endpoint, the application-control agent is the PEP for the question of whether code may run.'
notes.title: NIST SP 800-207: the logical model (PE, PA, PEP)

notes.body: Every security control is either default-allow (permit unless explicitly blocked) or default-deny (block unless explicitly permitted), and the choice decides who does the hard work: the defender or the attacker. Default-allow puts the burden on the defender to enumerate badness. Antivirus signatures, blocklists, firewall deny rules — all of these require you to know about the threat in advance, name it, and push the rule before the threat arrives. The attacker only needs one thing you have not seen yet: a fresh hash, a new domain, a renamed binary. This is an asymmetric game you lose by construction, because the space of 'unknown bad' is infinite and your blocklist is finite. Default-deny flips the burden. The policy enumerates goodness — the finite, knowable set of applications your business actually uses — and everything else is denied without needing to be recognized. The attacker's novel malware is not blocked because it is known-bad; it is blocked because it is not known-good, which requires zero threat intelligence about that specific sample. Worked example: a finance team uses 40 applications. Under default-allow, the defender must maintain rules against millions of malware families and hope the next one is recognized. Under default-deny, the defender maintains 40 allow entries and the next malware fails at the gate unrecognized — which is fine, because recognition was never required. Now the honest costs, because default-deny is not free. First, someone must build and maintain the allowlist: discover what is used, approve it, handle updates. Second, the first weeks are noisy: legitimate apps get blocked and users complain, so you need a fast approval workflow or the business routes around you. Third, allowlisting the application is necessary but not sufficient — a trusted app can be abused, which is exactly why ringfencing exists (Module M03) and why you should never present allowlisting as the whole answer. The classic mistake is treating default-deny as 'set and forget.' It is a living policy: every software update changes hashes, every new hire needs new apps, every acquired company brings unknown software. Operator habit: measure your policy's health by the approval queue's age. A queue of pending approvals older than your SLA is not a backlog; it is users learning to work around security. In the interview, when they ask why ThreatLocker leads with allowlisting, the answer is this economics argument in two sentences: default-allow forces defenders to enumerate infinite badness; default-deny enumerates finite goodness, so unknown threats fail closed with no signature required.
notes.title: Default-allow vs default-deny: the economics of the two models

notes.body: Assume breach is the psychological core of zero trust: design as though the attacker is already inside. This is not pessimism; it is engineering discipline. If you assume the perimeter will fail — because it will, via phishing, a vendor compromise, or a zero-day — then every internal system must defend itself, every lateral path must be gated, and every credential must be treated as stealable. The practical consequences for an endpoint operator are concrete. First, blast radius: assume any single machine can be compromised, so design so that one compromised machine cannot become ten. That means workstation-to-workstation traffic is denied by default (you will build this in M06), local admin is removed (M04), and data cannot walk out on a USB stick (M05). Second, no implicit trust between services: the accounting app server does not trust requests just because they arrive from the office subnet; each request is authenticated and authorized. Third, continuous diagnostics and mitigation: you do not audit quarterly and hope; you monitor the enforcement points continuously and treat every blocked action as a signal (that signal pipeline is M07). Worked example: two designs for a 200-seat company. Design A trusts the LAN: flat network, local admins everywhere, file shares open to 'Authenticated Users.' One phished credential gives the attacker the workstation, the admin hash gives them the domain, the open shares give them the data. Mean time from one click to domain-wide ransomware: hours. Design B assumes breach: workstations cannot talk to each other, no local admins, applications allowlisted and ringfenced, USB blocked, egress filtered. The same phished credential yields one isolated workstation whose malicious child processes are blocked at launch, whose lateral movement hits closed ports, and whose exfiltration hits closed egress. The attacker still got in — assume breach concedes that — but the breach stays a single-machine event instead of a company event. The operator gotcha is treating assume breach as a slogan on a slide. It is a test you run against every design: 'if this machine is already owned, what can the attacker reach from here?' If the answer is 'everything,' you do not have zero trust yet; you have a perimeter with extra steps. Make that question a habit and you will naturally produce the policies this course teaches you to build.  One more operational habit: test your assume-breach posture with tabletop exercises, not just architecture diagrams. Pick a scenario — 'the CFO's laptop is compromised right now' — and walk the team through what the attacker can reach from that machine in the first hour. If the honest answer includes the file server, the backup system, or the domain controller, the design has gaps regardless of what the slide deck claims. Run this exercise quarterly; the gaps it finds become the next quarter's policy projects, which is how assume breach turns from a mindset into a roadmap.
notes.title: Assume breach: the mindset that makes the architecture work

notes.body: In the NIST model the PEP is abstract — it can be a gateway, a proxy, an agent. On the endpoint, the application-control agent is the PEP for the most fundamental question a machine can be asked: may this code execute? Everything else the platform does hangs off that gate. Allowlisting (Application Control) is deny-by-default execution: when a process launch is requested, the agent checks identity — hash, certificate, path — against policy and permits only what is explicitly allowed. Ringfencing then constrains what the allowed application may do once running: which child processes it may spawn, whether it may touch the registry, which files it may read or write, which network connections it may open. Elevation Control decides whether the application may run with administrative rights, removing standing local admin and granting just-in-time elevation per policy. Storage Control and Network Control extend the same deny-by-default logic to data paths and network paths. Detect turns every block into an alert, and Configuration Manager keeps the underlying Defender baseline from drifting. See the pattern: each module takes one abuse path and flips it from default-allow to default-deny. The operator insight is that these modules are not seven separate products; they are one policy engine applied to seven questions: may it run, what may it do, with what privilege, where may data go, where may packets go, what was blocked, and is the baseline intact? Worked example: map a single attack chain to the gates. Phishing email delivers a malicious document. Gate 1 (allowlisting): the document's embedded payload tries to drop an unknown executable — blocked, not on the allowlist. Suppose instead the payload is a malicious macro inside an allowed Office app — it passes gate 1 because Word itself is allowed. Gate 2 (ringfencing): the macro tries to spawn PowerShell — Word's ringfence denies child process creation. Suppose the macro instead tries to write to a startup folder — gate 2 denies the file write. Suppose the attacker pivots to credential theft — gate 3 (elevation): no local admin, no privileged foothold. Exfiltration over USB — gate 4 (storage): device blocked. Callback to attacker infrastructure — gate 5 (network): egress denied for the unapproved process. Every step of the kill chain meets a default-deny gate, and each block emits a Detect alert. Common gotcha: presenting the modules as overlapping or redundant. They are layered: each assumes the previous layer can be bypassed and catches what falls through. That is defense in depth expressed as policy, and it is the answer when the panel asks 'isn't allowlisting enough?'
notes.title: The endpoint as enforcement point: how allowlisting fits the model

notes.body: Let us trace the same attack against two endpoints, minute by minute, and watch where each model breaks. The scenario: at 9:02 AM, an accountant opens what looks like a vendor invoice. The document contains a malicious macro. This is a generic pattern — no exotic zero-day, just the commodity attack chain that encrypts companies every week. Against the default-allow endpoint: 9:02:14, the macro executes because Office macros are permitted and nothing evaluates the payload. 9:02:31, the macro drops invoice_helper.exe into the user's temp folder and launches it — no gate checks whether this binary is known-good. 9:03:05, the binary disables shadow copies and begins enumerating network shares; the endpoint firewall allows outbound SMB to neighbors because workstation-to-workstation traffic was never restricted. 9:04:40, it contacts its command server over HTTPS — egress is default-allow, so the callback succeeds. 9:06:12, encryption begins on local files and mapped shares. 9:07:00, the antivirus finally flags the binary by signature — forty-five seconds after the damage started, and the signature only exists because someone else was hit first. Total defender actions before detonation: zero. The model required the threat to be known, and it was not known in time. Against the default-deny endpoint: 9:02:14, the macro attempts to spawn a child process — the Office application's ringfence policy denies child process creation for winword.exe, and the attempt is logged. 9:02:15, the macro's fallback tries to write an executable to the temp folder — the ringfence denies the file write outside approved paths. 9:02:16, suppose the attacker anticipated this and the payload instead arrives as a standalone executable the user is tricked into running: the allowlisting PEP checks the binary's hash and certificate against policy — unknown, so execution is denied before a single instruction runs. 9:02:17, Detect fires an alert: blocked child-process spawn from winword.exe on ACCOUNTING-07. The SOC now has a lead at the attempt stage, not the encryption stage. 9:03:00, even if every application-layer gate somehow failed, the endpoint firewall's default-deny inbound rules block the SMB enumeration of neighbors, and egress filtering blocks the unknown binary's callback. The attack dies at the first gate it meets, and there are five gates. The teaching point is not that default-deny is magic — a sufficiently privileged, signed, allowed application abused in a permitted way can still cause harm, which is why the layers overlap. The point is the shift in who needs to be perfect: default-allow needs the defender to recognize every novel threat before it acts; default-deny needs the attacker to be running explicitly approved code behaving within its fence. Study this trace until you can whiteboard it. The panel will very likely ask some version of 'walk me through what happens when ransomware hits a protected endpoint,' and this minute-by-minute telling — attempt, block, alert, containment — is the answer that shows operator thinking instead of marketing recall.
notes.title: Worked example: ransomware detonation, default-allow vs default-deny

notes.body: Here is the truth that separates operators from tool buyers: in a deny-by-default world, the policy is the product. The agent is just the enforcement mechanism; the value — and the risk — lives in the rules you write, the approvals you grant, and the exceptions you allow to rot. A sloppy allowlist with a standing 'allow everything from the downloads folder' exception is default-allow wearing a default-deny costume. So the operational discipline has four parts. First, policy authorship: every rule needs an owner, a business justification, a scope (which users, which machines, which groups), and an expiry or review date. 'Allow chrome.exe' is not a rule; 'Allow Google Chrome stable, publisher Google LLC, for the Sales group, reviewed quarterly' is a rule. Second, change management: application updates change hashes, so your policy must handle trusted updaters — the vendor's own update mechanism — or every Patch Tuesday becomes a company-wide outage. You will design updater rules in M02; internalize now that update handling is the number-one operational burden of allowlisting and the number-one place junior operators get burned. Third, the approval workflow: when a user hits a block on legitimate software, the path from block to approval must be measured in minutes or hours, not days. A slow approval process teaches users that security is the department of 'no,' and they will find workarounds — personal devices, shadow IT — that are worse than the risk you were managing. Fourth, exception hygiene: every temporary exception ('allow this unsigned installer for the migration weekend') gets a ticket, an owner, and an automatic expiry. Review the exception list monthly; exceptions that outlive their justification become permanent holes. Worked example: the accounting office needs a new payroll app. The operator verifies the publisher certificate, checks the vendor's published hash, scopes the rule to the accounting group, sets a 90-day review, and documents the business justification in the ticket. The app updates itself monthly via its own updater — so the operator adds a trusted-updater rule for the vendor's signed updater rather than re-approving every version. When the panel asks 'how do you keep allowlisting from breaking the business,' this is the answer: updater rules for the churn, a fast approval lane for the new, scoped rules with reviews for everything, and exceptions that expire. Common gotcha: writing policy for the lab and forgetting policy for the humans. The workflow around the policy — who approves, how fast, what evidence — matters as much as the rules themselves.
notes.title: Policy as the product: the operational discipline

summary: Zero trust is not a product you buy; it is a design discipline that removes implicit trust from the network and from the endpoint. This module maps NIST SP 800-207's logical model (policy engine, policy administrator, policy enforcement point) to what actually runs on a workstation, and shows why deny-by-default is the only sane enforcement posture once you assume breach.
title: Zero Trust Deny-by-Default Architecture
